items.title: The Cartesian Equation of an Ellipse

sections.normalized_html: Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse [MATH: x= 4\cos\theta,\quad y=2\sin\theta - 1, \quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.]
sections.readable_text:
Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse
[MATH: x= 4\cos\theta,\quad y=2\sin\theta - 1, \quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.]

sections.normalized_html:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter [MATH: \theta.] We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the [MATH: \cos\theta] term in the [MATH: x]-equation and squaring, we get

[MATH: x|= 4\cos θ; (x)/(4)|= \cos θ; (x^{2})/(4^{2})|= \cos^{2} θ; (x^{2})/(16)|= \cos^{2} θ.] By isolating the [MATH: \sin\theta] term in the [MATH: y]-equation and squaring, we get [MATH: y + 1|= 2\sin θ; (y + 1)/(2)|= \sin θ; ((y + 1)^{2})/(2^{2})|= \sin^{2} θ; ((y + 1)^{2})/(4)|= \sin^{2} θ.] Adding the two equations and using [MATH: \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta =1,] we get [MATH: (x^{2})/(16) + ((y + 1)^{2})/(4)|= \cos^{2} θ + \sin^{2} θ = 1.] So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is [MATH: \frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{(y+1)^2}{4} = 1.]

[MATH: x|= 4\cos θ; (x)/(4)|= \cos θ; (x^{2})/(4^{2})|= \cos^{2} θ; (x^{2})/(16)|= \cos^{2} θ.]
By isolating the [MATH: \sin\theta] term in the [MATH: y]-equation and squaring, we get
[MATH: y + 1|= 2\sin θ; (y + 1)/(2)|= \sin θ; ((y + 1)^{2})/(2^{2})|= \sin^{2} θ; ((y + 1)^{2})/(4)|= \sin^{2} θ.]
Adding the two equations and using [MATH: \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta =1,] we get
[MATH: (x^{2})/(16) + ((y + 1)^{2})/(4)|= \cos^{2} θ + \sin^{2} θ = 1.]
So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is
[MATH: \frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{(y+1)^2}{4} = 1.]

Item 11 — Example: The Cartesian Equation of an Ellipse

Example Prompt:
Find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse
[MATH: x= 4\cos\theta,\quad y=2\sin\theta - 1, \quad 0\leq\theta<2\pi.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find the Cartesian equation of the ellipse, we need to eliminate the parameter [MATH: \theta.] We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the [MATH: \cos\theta] term in the [MATH: x]-equation and squaring, we get

[MATH: x|= 4\cos θ; (x)/(4)|= \cos θ; (x^{2})/(4^{2})|= \cos^{2} θ; (x^{2})/(16)|= \cos^{2} θ.]
By isolating the [MATH: \sin\theta] term in the [MATH: y]-equation and squaring, we get
[MATH: y + 1|= 2\sin θ; (y + 1)/(2)|= \sin θ; ((y + 1)^{2})/(2^{2})|= \sin^{2} θ; ((y + 1)^{2})/(4)|= \sin^{2} θ.]
Adding the two equations and using [MATH: \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta =1,] we get
[MATH: (x^{2})/(16) + ((y + 1)^{2})/(4)|= \cos^{2} θ + \sin^{2} θ = 1.]
So the Cartesian equation of the ellipse is
[MATH: \frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{(y+1)^2}{4} = 1.]
